title: Variational Mode Decomposition: Building the Solver, and Measuring What Hindsight Buys

Introduction
Price is a sum of things happening at different speeds: a multi-month trend, a multi-week swing, an intraday wobble, and noise that means nothing. Every trader draws that decomposition by eye on every change of timeframe. The question here is whether a machine can draw it, and what the drawing is worth once drawn.
The standard answers are unsatisfying. A moving average extracts a trend but lags it, throws the rest away, and needs you to pick the lookback. A Fourier transform assumes the frequencies never change, which is false for any market. Empirical Mode Decomposition is adaptive and popular, but it is a recipe rather than a stated problem and it suffers from mode mixing, one component quietly absorbing part of another.
Variational Mode Decomposition
(Dragomiretskiy and Zosso, 2014) states a clear optimization: find K components that sum to the signal, each as narrow as possible around its own center frequency. It is solved by the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and yields clean bands with directly readable center frequencies. There is no VMD implementation on this site, so this article writes one.
The library is the first half; the second half decided how it had to be built. VMD is a batch algorithm: hand it a series and it optimizes over the whole thing at once, so a naive implementation decomposes the full chart history and plots the modes. The result looks convincing, fitting most historical turning points, and it is worthless, because every historical bar's mode value came from a window containing that bar's own future. This article measures how much of that picture is hindsight, on three real symbol/timeframe combinations against matched random walks.
You will end with a working library, an indicator whose every plotted point is computed once from a window ending at its own bar, a strategy whose stop, target and holding time come from the decomposition rather than from taste, and a set of numbers telling you what to believe.
What this delivers
The indicator draws three things on the main chart: the denoised signal, the trend mode alone, and a band showing how far this market currently wanders for no reason. A panel carries every mode's period in bars, its share of the energy, and a verdict on whether the window was solved well enough to read.
Fig. 1. The indicator on XAUUSD D1: every plotted point comes from a window ending at that bar, and the panel reports the modes and the solve quality
That is the visible product; the measured one matters more. Decomposing the whole visible history in one call, which almost every published VMD chart does, and comparing it bar by bar against the causal version gives this:

A batch chart is not a smoother version of the causal one. On roughly one bar in three, across the three combinations tested, it points the other way. That table is why the indicator in Fig. 1 is built the way it is.
Fig. 2. The same trend mode computed two ways over the same bars, with the disagreement in direction shaded
The method: what VMD actually solves
VMD asks for K modes u_k that add up to the input f, each concentrated around its own center frequency w_k. "Concentrated" is made precise by taking each mode's analytic signal, shifting it to baseband, and penalizing the squared norm of its time derivative. A narrow band changes slowly once shifted down, so a small penalty means a tight mode.
Written out, the constrained problem is:
minimize over {u_k},{w_k}: sum_k || d/dt [ analytic(u_k)(t) * exp(-j*w_k*t) ] ||^
2
subject to sum_k u_k = f
The constraint is handled with an augmented Lagrangian, which adds a quadratic penalty and a dual variable lambda, and is solved by alternating: hold everything else fixed and update one block at a time. In the frequency domain each update has a closed form, which makes VMD cheap despite looking heavy.
Updating mode k is a Wiener filter on whatever the other modes have not explained:
u_k(w) = ( f(w) - sum_{i != k} u_i(w) -
lambda
(w)/
2
) / (
1
+ alpha*(w - w_k)^
2
)
The denominator is the whole idea. At w = w_k it equals 1 and the residual passes through untouched; far from w_k it grows as alpha times the squared distance and crushes whatever is there. So alpha sets how wide each band may be.
The center frequency is the power-weighted centroid of the mode just built:
w_k = sum_w w*|u_k(w)|^
2
/ sum_w |u_k(w)|^
2
The dual variable takes an ascent step on how badly the modes fail to add up:
lambda
(w) =
lambda
(w) + tau*( sum_k u_k(w) - f(w) )
Three parameters fall out.
K
is how many modes you want.
alpha
is the bandwidth penalty, so a large alpha gives narrow, well-separated bands.
tau
is the dual ascent step, and setting it to zero relaxes the sum-to-signal constraint, the right choice when the input is noisy.
Fig. 3 shows this on a signal where the answer is known: three cosines at 4, 16 and 48 cycles across the window, summed, then handed to the solver with no hint about what went in.
Fig. 3. A sum of three tones and the three modes the solver pulls back out of it, with the recovered cycle counts
The library recovers 4.000, 15.999 and 48.001 cycles, the sanity check every decomposition should pass before it is pointed at price.
The frequency-domain plumbing
Every update above is a pointwise operation on a spectrum; nothing in the iteration transforms anything. The input is transformed once before the loop and the K finished modes once after it, so a decomposition costs K+1 transforms however many iterations it runs. The iteration count, not the transform, sets the price.
The transform is an iterative radix-2 Cooley-Tukey in VMDTransform.mqh. Two details in it are easy to get wrong.
First, twiddle factors are evaluated with cosine and sine per butterfly rather than carried as a running product. The running product is faster but accumulates drift, and that drift feeds back into the solver: the filter divides by
1 + alpha*(w - w_k)^2
and w_k is a power-weighted centroid of the same spectrum.
Second, the shift that moves the zero frequency to the middle of the array is its own inverse at even length, being nothing but a swap of the two halves, which is why the library has one routine rather than a forward and inverse pair:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Move the zero frequency to the middle of the array               |
//|                                                                  |
//|  For an EVEN length this is just a swap of the two halves, and   |
//|  that operation is its own inverse - which is why forward and    |
//|  inverse shifts are one routine here rather than two. Odd        |
//|  lengths would need the usual off-by-one pair, and are refused:  |
//|  the solver only ever shifts arrays of length T = 2N.            |
//|                                                                  |
//|  After the shift, index T/2 carries the zero frequency, indices  |
//|  below it the negative frequencies and indices above it the      |
//|  positive ones. The solver relies on exactly that layout when it |
//|  zeroes the negative half to build the analytic signal.          |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+

Before the transform runs, the window is mirrored. With h = N/2, the first h bars are reflected onto the front and the last h onto the back, so a window of N bars is actually solved at length T = 2N. Without it the first and last bars look like a discontinuity to a periodic transform, and every mode picks up a spurious jump there. With it the extended array is continuous across the original window's ends, though not smooth: reflection reverses the slope at each join, so the mirror removes the step and leaves a kink. The step is the part the spectrum reacts to most.
That has a consequence that comes back in the results. The ends of the window are the least trustworthy part of any decomposition, since half their supporting data is reflection rather than observation, and in trading the end of the window is the only part you can act on.

After the shift, the negative half of the spectrum is zeroed. That converts the real signal to its analytic counterpart, which is what the derivation assumes, and it means every mode the solver produces is one-sided too. The Hermitian symmetry is put back by hand at the end, before the inverse transform. The construction is a little more than a dropped half-array: the Nyquist bin lands at index 0 and is zeroed with the negative frequencies, the surviving bins keep their original amplitudes rather than being doubled, and the zero-frequency bin survives carrying almost nothing because the mean was already removed.
Because the transform is radix-2 and the solve happens at T = 2N, N must be a power of two. There is no zero-padding escape here of the kind a convolution enjoys. That is not because padding changes the spectrum while mirroring does not, since both change it, but because they change it differently: zeros append a flat segment unrelated to the series, while the reflection appends samples with the same local level and variance. No measurement here puts a number on that gap. The data layer therefore snaps a requested window down to the nearest power of two.
Fig. 4. The window is reflected to twice its length before transforming, and the negative half of the centered spectrum is discarded
The ADMM solver
The solver lives in VMDCore.mqh. Its inner sweep is the three updates from Section 3 over K modes; the excerpt below is the mode update: the accumulator, the Wiener filter, the centroid.

The accumulator deserves a note. Updating mode k naively needs the sum of all the other modes, a fresh O(K*T) sum for every mode on every sweep. Instead m_sumRe is carried across the run and corrected by two terms: add the mode that just moved out of the "others" set, subtract the one moving in. That mixes the already-updated modes of this sweep with the previous sweep's rest, which is the Gauss-Seidel ordering the method expects. Whether the running sum is right is not visible here: it also depends on the initial fill before the first sweep and on the row swap that makes P the previous sweep and C the current one, both outside this loop. The tests check the consequence, planted tones at the right frequencies, not the recurrence alone.
The indices
P
and
C
are the second thing worth pointing at. The reference stores all iterations in an array of size maxIter x 2N x K, about 32 MB per call at N = 512 and K = 4. The recurrence never reads further back than one sweep, so this solver keeps two rolling rows and swaps them: the same arithmetic in roughly 130 KB, which matters because a rolling indicator calls it once per bar.
One inherited quirk is reproduced deliberately. The reference reads its answer from the
second to last
ADMM row rather than the last one, a detail carried down from the original MATLAB. It is what every published VMD result was produced with, so the solver matches it, and removing it shifts the output by a small amount that looks exactly like a tolerance problem in a cross-check and is not one. That is a compatibility decision and only that: matching the reference says nothing about which row is the better answer, since near convergence the two differ by less than the tolerance.
Convergence is not guaranteed, and one series will not show you how often it fails
. Over 40 walks at N = 512, K = 4, alpha = 2000 and tol = 1e-6, 35 converged out of 40, with the iteration count spanning 71 to 499 and a median of 218. So roughly one window in eight runs out of iterations, which makes the converged flag a live quality gate, not a formality.
Both K and alpha buy convergence, and alpha is the sharper.

A small alpha means wide bands that overlap and fight, the least stable setting available. A large K costs twice over, for the extra modes and the extra sweeps they need.
Fig. 5. Iteration counts over 40 matched random walks, and how the converged fraction moves with the bandwidth penalty
The cost that follows from all this is set by the iteration count. Each sweep is linear in N at fixed K while the K+1 transforms outside the loop are N log N, so the sweeps dominate at these window sizes; at much larger N the transforms would begin to show. In MetaTrader 5, as the minimum over five repetitions, one ADMM iteration costs about 44, 79 and 144 microseconds at N = 256, 512 and 1024 with K = 4; three runs of the same test reported those numbers as high as 61, 98 and 261. The minimum is a lower bound on the solver's cost, not the latency to expect, and the test reports no median or tail, so plan against the upper figures. The spread is most likely contention with other terminal activity, but that is a reading rather than a measurement: no profiling or isolated replay was run. At the shipped tolerance a price window runs about 150 to 270 iterations, so one decomposition lands near 12 to 26 milliseconds at N = 512. Loosening the tolerance from 1e-9 to 1e-4 saves about 40% of that and moves the answer by 0.095% of range, which is why 1e-4 is the default.
Important:
GetTickCount cannot time this: its resolution on Windows is about 15 ms, the same order as a whole decomposition, and it reported 0, 15 and 15 ms for three runs that differed by a factor of four. Use GetMicrosecondCount and print the observed range.
The causal boundary, and testing it by sabotage
Everything so far decomposes an array. Which array it is allowed to see is the decision that makes the library usable, and it lives in one class rather than in the indicator and the strategy.
CVMDData takes a bar anchor and produces the window ending at that bar, transformed three ways. Prices are log-transformed, because a 1% move should count the same at 2000 as at 3000 and because mode amplitudes then read directly as fractional moves, which is where the strategy's target comes from. Then the mean is removed, then the length is snapped to a power of two.
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| One window from the chart, anchored at a bar SHIFT               |
//|                                                                  |
//|  endShift is a shift, so 1 is the last CLOSED bar and 0 is the   |
//|  bar still forming. Callers that pass 0 are decomposing a bar    |
//|  that is still changing, and every reading taken from it will    |
//|  change with it; the library allows it but the indicator and the |
//|  EA both anchor at 1 on purpose.                                 |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+

Removing the mean is free mathematically, since subtracting a constant moves only the zero-frequency term, and arithmetically it is the difference between a working library and a broken one: the mean of log gold is an enormous spike at the exact center of the spectrum, it survives the analytic-signal step, and every mode's Wiener filter then fights over it. The removed mean is kept so a caller can map a mode value back to price.
Now the part that matters

The measured difference is 0.000e+00 on both the modes and the frequencies. The test then does the opposite check, moving the anchor bar itself by 5% and demanding the answer
does
change, because a function that ignores its input would also pass the first half. Two limits on what that proves. Comparing against zero exactly is right inside one process on one build, where both calls take identical arithmetic paths, but it is not a benchmark that would survive a change of compiler. And it exercises the array path; the chart path is covered by the indicator verification in Section 10.
Reading a decomposition honestly
A decomposition always returns something: modes for a pure trend, for noise, and for a window where the solver quit without settling, and on a chart all three look equally convincing. So the numbers that say whether the answer means anything travel with it in the same struct.
int
K;
// number of modes
int
n;
// samples per mode
double
modes[];
// K*n, mode k at [k*n .. k*n+n-1]
double
omega[];
// K center frequencies, cycles per bar
double
energy[];
// K mode energies as a fraction of input
int
iters;
// ADMM iterations actually run
int
maxIters;
// the cap it was allowed
bool
converged;
// stopped by tolerance, not by the cap
double
uDiff;
// the convergence measure at the end
double
residFrac;
// unexplained energy / input energy
double
residMaxAbs;
// largest single-sample residual
double
minGapCycles;
// smallest adjacent omega gap, in cycles
bool
omegaSorted;
// did the solver return them in order
bool
valid;
// the inputs were accepted at all
Three of these need explaining.
residFrac is not an epsilon check
. The obvious property to assert is that the modes sum back to the input, which is the constraint the problem states, and the solver meets it exactly at no tau: at tau = 0 the constraint is deliberately relaxed, and with tau non-zero the dual ascent drives the sum toward the input without arriving, because the Wiener filters have finite bandwidth and some energy never lands in any mode. A three-tone signal leaves 8.7e-03 even at tau = 1.0, and a random walk leaves about 3% of range. Over 40 walks at K = 4 the unexplained fraction is 5.8e-03 at the median and 1.2e-02 at the ninetieth percentile, and the shipped threshold sits above that percentile: an empirical setting from forty walks at one window length, not a derived bound, with its stability across windows and instruments untested.
minGapCycles is the K selection signal
. Ask for more modes than the signal supports and two collapse onto the same frequency, at which point the pair is one mode reported twice. On one walk the smallest gap between adjacent center frequencies held between 3.5 and 4.8 cycles from K = 2 through K = 6 and then fell to 1.43 at K = 7, while the residual stopped improving. That collapse is the signal that K is too large, and it is reported per window rather than baked into a rule, because the collapse point is series dependent: other walks hold their separation to K = 8 and never collapse at all. So there is no K that is right in general and no rejection rule here either; what is reproducible is the procedure, which is to sweep K on your own series and stop before the smallest gap collapses while the residual stops improving.
Mode order is not guaranteed
. With uniform frequency initialization the planted tones at 4, 16 and 48 cycles came back in the order 4, 48, 16, and on one walk it invented a 156-cycle mode where zero initialization gave a sensible spread. The facade therefore rebuilds a frequency ranking after every decomposition and every accessor works in rank, so rank 0 is the slowest component whatever index the solver gave.
Fig. 6. The smallest gap between adjacent modes against K, on two random walks: one collapses past the usable level at K = 7, the other holds its separation throughout
On top of these the facade exposes four readings a strategy may use, each derived from the decomposition rather than chosen: a mode's swing amplitude (its root mean square times the square root of two, exact for a sinusoid), its half period in bars, the noise width, the standard deviation of everything the denoised signal dropped, and a regime ratio.
That last one needs stating, because the obvious regime measure fails on price: log price is dominated by its trend, so rank 0 carried 95.7% of the energy on XAUUSD D1, the slow-energy reading came out at 0.9932, and a gate at 0.90 would pass every window ever presented to it. Dropping rank 0 and asking about the rest gives a number with room to move:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Oscillatory structure against oscillatory churn, trend EXCLUDED  |
//|                                                                  |
//|  SlowEnergy is the obvious regime reading and on price data it   |
//|  is nearly useless, which only a real chart showed: log price is |
//|  dominated by its trend, so rank 0 carried 95.7% of the energy   |
//|  on XAUUSD D1 and SlowEnergy(2) read 0.9932. A gate at 0.90      |
//|  would pass every window ever presented to it.                   |
//|                                                                  |
//|  This ratio drops rank 0 entirely and asks the question that is  |
//|  actually open: of the part of the move that is NOT the trend,   |
//|  how much sits in slow swings rather than in fast churn. On the  |
//|  same XAUUSD window that is 1.07% against 0.46% + 0.20%, a ratio |
//|  of about 1.6 - a number with room to move in both directions.   |
//|                                                                  |
//|  Returns 0 when there is no oscillatory energy at all, and a     |
//|  large finite number rather than infinity when there is no       |
//|  churn, so a caller can compare it without special cases.        |

Whether that is worth gating on is what the next two sections answer.
Checking the solver against a reference
A from-scratch numerical solver is worth as much as its verification. VMD is lucky here: the widely used Python reference (
vmdpy
) is fully deterministic, its center frequencies starting either at zero or at a fixed uniform spread with no random seeding, which turns the cross-check from a statistical comparison into an equality.
The verification uses two Python implementations. The first is the reference itself. The second is restructured the way the MQL5 code had to be written: two rolling ADMM rows instead of a full history, a hand-written radix-2 transform instead of a library call, real arrays instead of complex ones. Checking against both separates two failures. Agreeing with the reference but not the restructured version means the port drifted; the reverse means the blueprint was wrong to begin with.
An MQL5 script exports eleven configurations, dumping the window the solver saw along with its modes, frequencies and diagnostics. Doubles are written with
%.
17g, which round-trips an IEEE 754 double exactly, so the comparison is made at the level of the arithmetic rather than at six decimals; that assumes a period decimal separator, and on a comma-decimal environment the Python side splits the row on the wrong character and fails outright rather than quietly shifting a digit. The cases exercise every branch: both initializations, the zero-frequency constraint on and off, tau zero and non-zero, three window sizes, four values of K, and two windows of real gold bars.

The iteration count matching exactly on every case is the strongest line in that table. The two implementations did not merely arrive at the same answer, they took the same number of steps to get there, which requires the convergence measure to track closely enough at every sweep to cross the tolerance on the same one. That is not agreement at the last digit: two runs that differ slightly can still cross a threshold together.
Alongside the reference comparison the suite checks things that need no reference: the transform against a direct O(N^2) discrete transform, against closed forms for a constant, an impulse and a pure cosine, and against Parseval's identity and linearity. Those catch what an equality check cannot, both implementations being wrong in the same way.
What hindsight buys
Here is the experiment the library was built for.
Roll a causal decomposition forward one bar at a time and record, for each anchor, the trend value assigned to the bar at the window's edge and to the bars behind it. A bar gets one value as the newest bar in the window, and a different one once it is one, five or twenty-five bars old. The gap between them is repaint.
The comparison needs a null, so here is the null. Each matched walk is built in log space from the real series' own per-bar log-return standard deviation, with no drift term, from a fixed-seed linear congruential stream whose draws are six uniforms summed to unit variance. It carries gold's volatility but neither its trend nor its tails, and the same seed reproduces every number here. The repaint table uses one such walk and the regime band five. The forty behind the convergence table in Section 5, which are also the forty behind the residual percentiles in Section 7, are a simpler null: plain unit-variance Gaussian walks from the Python phase, matched to no instrument, because neither convergence nor the residual floor is a property of a symbol.

The endpoint profile answers a related question badly. Drift from the freshest reading grows roughly linearly with distance from the window edge, out to the 50 bars measured, with no sign of stabilization: on XAUUSD D1 it runs 17, 35, 54, 64, 81 basis points at one through five bars back and keeps climbing. There is no lag at which the reading settles.
The practical response is to compute each point once, from the window ending at its own bar, and never recompute it. That plot does not repaint, not because repaint was engineered away, but because the real-time estimate is what gets drawn and is then left alone. Two senses of the word are worth keeping apart: causal means the value uses no bar after its own, which the data layer enforces and the sabotage test checks, but it is not stable, since the value sits at the window edge where half its support is reflection. Drawing it once fixes the picture, not the uncertainty.

The scope of this should be read off the design. Three symbol and timeframe combinations, 250 rolling anchors each, one matched walk behind the repaint table and five behind the regime band: every number above is a point estimate with no confidence interval, no p-value and no bootstrap behind it, and the percentages are quoted more precisely than the sample supports. That is enough to show that batch and causal readings differ by a lot, and that a series with no cycles drifts by a similar amount. It is not enough to put a figure on either difference, or to say whether the pattern survives on instruments not looked at.
None of this makes the decomposition useless. It makes it descriptive. The modes are a well-defined and reproducible summary of what a window contains, and the noise width is a genuine volatility estimate. What the measurements refuse is the leap from "this is a clean decomposition" to "this tells me something the market did not already say."
The indicator
VMD_Decomposition.mq5 plots four buffers on the main chart: the denoised signal, the trend mode, and a band at plus and minus a chosen number of noise standard deviations around the denoised line, all mapped back through the log and the removed mean so they sit in price units. One caution about reading them: the modes add in log space, not in price, so exponentiating one mode does not give a price component that the others add to. The trend line is that mode's level expressed as a price, not a split of price into additive parts.
The important part is the calculation policy. On the first pass it wipes every buffer and computes each displayed bar once from its own causal window; on every later call it computes only newly closed bars. A value already written is never recomputed.

The history cap is a cost decision, not a convention. One decomposition costs a few milliseconds and a first load pays that once per displayed bar. Measured on this build the default of 150 bars took 1017 ms on XAUUSD D1 (6.8 ms per bar) and 222 ms on EURUSD H1 (1.5 ms per bar), each the fastest of several loads; the slowest of the same loads were 1244 ms and 352 ms, which are the figures to plan against. A 500-bar setting would be three times worse for no extra information, since the older bars carry the reading they would have carried anyway.
The panel is drawn with chart objects, a background rectangle plus text labels, rather than Comment. That is the only way to get aligned columns and a readable box, but chart objects do not clip their text: a value too long for the panel renders out over the chart, and no buffer assertion can see that because buffers know nothing about labels. Any long value is therefore wrapped at a character count derived from the panel width and font size, and the panel reports the widest label it drew so an overflow announces itself in the log. That is a log-level guard and not a visual assertion: nothing inspects the rendered panel, so the last check on its geometry is the eye.
Because an indicator cannot assert on itself, VMD_Verify_Indicator.mq5 drives it through iCustom and checks the buffers from outside: that exactly the display window is filled and older bars left empty, that the band brackets the denoised line, that the values sit in price range rather than log units, that the denoised line is smoother than price, and that the forming bar mirrors the last closed one instead of leading it.
Its last check is the one that matters. The script decomposes the same bar itself and compares its answer against what the indicator plotted there; if those agree, the plotted point came from a window ending at its own bar. On XAUUSD D1 and EURUSD H1 the worst disagreement across five probe bars was 0.000e+00. That is five probe bars on two charts at the shipped settings: strong evidence about the path the indicator takes, silent about very small windows, too little history, or a symbol change mid-session.

The stop is a multiple of the noise width, the measured spread of everything the decomposition could not explain, so it scales with how far this market is wandering for no reason. The target is a multiple of the traded mode's own amplitude, and the holding limit a multiple of that mode's half period, which is how long a swing of that frequency takes to complete. Position size then risks a fixed fraction of equity across the stop distance.
Every number below comes from one configuration, stated so it can be reproduced: a 512-bar window, K = 4, alpha = 2000, tol = 1e-4, a stop at two noise standard deviations, a target of one cycle amplitude, a time stop of one half period capped at 200 bars, and one percent of equity risked per trade. The window is worth naming out loud: 512 is what the indicator ships with and what every measurement here was made at, and it matters more than the trade logic.
The quality gates from Section 7 do refuse windows. Over a four and a half year run on gold H1 the strategy saw 27023 bars and refused 273 for unexplained energy above the threshold, none for modes too close together and none for a solve that never converged. The rule doing most of the work is trend agreement: of 1030 zero crossings, 589 were rejected for disagreeing with the trend mode and 3 more arrived while a position was already open, leaving 436 entries. Every signal that did not become a trade is counted and printed.
Fig. 9. Balance and equity over 436 trades, XAUUSD H1 from January 2022 to August 2026, at a 512-bar window and a target of one cycle amplitude
The tester puts numbers on that curve: 436 trades for a net 2240.27 on a 10000 deposit, a profit factor of 1.15, 64.22% of trades profitable, an average win of 61.27 against an average loss of 95.61, and a maximum balance drawdown of 1491.76, or 13.31%. Winning two trades in three while the average loss is half again the average win is what a near target and a wide stop look like from the account's side. It is also a curve that goes up, which is the kind of result that gets published without the test that comes next.
Now the honest part. A balance curve on its own says almost nothing about whether the signal knows anything, so the strategy carries a diagnostic input that takes the opposite of every signal and changes nothing else. If following loses and fading wins by a similar amount, the signal carries real information with the wrong sign; if both lose by about the cost of trading, it carries none.

Following beats fading by 61.8 percentage points on the hourly chart and by 13.2 on the daily, on the same signals in each pair. That asymmetry, rather than the balance curve above it, is the result worth reporting, and it is also the whole of the claim. These are two paired runs on one instrument with no significance test behind the gap, and things other than the signal could produce it: the stop and target are not symmetric, so reversing an entry does not reverse the trade; the instrument trended over both periods; and both arms inherit the same spread and the same execution model. The reversal test rules out the laziest explanation for a rising curve. It does not establish an edge.
The daily row deserves a note. A 512-bar window on daily bars is two years of history, and the tester hands out only 314 bars before the test starts, so the first 202 bars produce no model at all and the EA says so in the log rather than silently doing nothing. Over 2022 to 2026 the same configuration reaches just 11 trades, which is why the row above starts in 2016, and even then ten and a half years yields only 47.
Fig. 10. Final balance from following the signal against fading it on gold, on the same trades in each pair
Important:
this is a result for one instrument, one broker's history and one configuration, and it is offered as exactly that. Nothing here claims the strategy is profitable on other symbols, and anyone with the attached files should run it themselves first. Two limits matter inside that scope. There is no out-of-sample period, because this broker's gold hourly history begins in January 2021, and no walk-forward either, so nothing re-selects the settings as the data moves. And the outcome moves a long way on a setting unrelated to the trade logic: the same instrument, period and target on a 256-bar window returns 9474, a loss of 5.3%. Report the asymmetry. Do not read the 22% as an edge.
That is the evidence, stated in full. On gold, over this period and on both timeframes tested, following the decomposition's direction did better than fading it. With no out-of-sample period, no walk-forward, and an outcome that changes sign when the window moves from 512 to 256, that describes two backtests rather than demonstrating a robust signal. The strategy is one section of this article rather than its subject: the library, the causal boundary and the measurement of what hindsight buys are what have to stand on their own.
Conclusion
Variational Mode Decomposition now exists for MetaTrader 5 as a from-scratch library, agreeing with a deterministic reference to 1.29e-13 on the modes, wrapped in a causal boundary tested by sabotage rather than asserted, and reported alongside the numbers that say when to distrust it.
What was built:
A radix-2 transform and centered-spectrum shift, checked against a direct O(N^2) transform, against closed forms, and against Parseval's identity and linearity.
The ADMM solver, in two rolling rows rather than a full iteration history, matching the Python reference to 1.29e-13 on the modes and taking the same number of iterations on all eleven exported test cases.
A data layer that owns the causal boundary, log transform, mean removal and power-of-two window, tested by overwriting the future and demanding an unchanged answer.
A result type that carries convergence, unexplained energy and mode separation, so a bad solve can be refused instead of plotted.
An indicator whose every plotted point is computed once from a window ending at its own bar, with an external script that reproduces those points independently.
A strategy whose stop comes from the noise width, target from the traded mode's amplitude and holding time from that mode's half period, with a diagnostic that separates a real signal from a spread bleed.
A measurement of what a batch decomposition adds, on three symbol and timeframe combinations against matched random walks.
The measurement is the part worth carrying away. On the three combinations looked at, a batch VMD chart is not a slightly optimistic version of the causal one: it points the other way on roughly a quarter to a third of bars, and a volatility-matched random walk drifts by a comparable amount. against: The trading signal uses the oscillatory mode (rank 1) crossing zero while the trend mode is rising — but the trend mode is computed from a causal window ending at the current bar, and its 'rising' condition requires comparing its value at the current bar to its value at the previous bar; however, the article states that 'the ends of the window are the least trustworthy part... since half their supporting data is reflection rather than observation', and crucially: the trend mode value at the *current bar* (i.e., the window's last point) is computed from a mirrored window where the last h bars are reflections of the first h bars — meaning the trend mode’s endpoint value is not based on observed price data beyond the anchor, but on artificial reflection. While this satisfies formal causality (no future *price* data), the trend’s 'rising' decision at the edge relies on a value contaminated by non-observational (mirrored) data — and the article explicitly warns that 'the end of the window is the only part you can act on' *and* 'the least trustworthy'. This violates robust causal usability: the signal’s core logic depends on the most unstable part of the decomposition.

The strategy’s stop, target, and holding time are derived from decomposition outputs (noise width, amplitude, half-period), but the noise width is defined as 'the standard deviation of everything the denoised signal dropped' — i.e., residuals from the VMD fit. However, the article states: 'the solver meets [the sum-to-signal constraint] exactly at no tau: at tau = 0 the constraint is deliberately relaxed, and with tau non-zero [...] some energy never lands in any mode'. It further reports unexplained energy fractions up to ~1.2e-2 (1.2%) for random walks and notes the shipped threshold sits 'above that percentile'. This means the 'noise' includes systematic unmodeled structure — not just stochastic noise — so using its std dev for stop placement assumes Gaussian/white noise properties unjustified by the method or data. The article itself calls the decomposition 'descriptive', not predictive, and refuses the leap to 'something the market did not already say'. Thus, the risk parameters lack a sound statistical foundation tied to actionable edge.

The entry condition 'rank 1 crosses up through zero while the trend mode is rising' is not fully specified as a deterministic formula: (a) 'crosses up through zero' implies discrete sampling — but the article never defines how zero-crossing is detected (e.g., sign change between bars? interpolation? hysteresis?), nor handles edge cases (e.g., multiple zero crossings within window, flat segments); (b) 'trend mode is rising' is ambiguous — rising over how many bars? 1? 2? SMA-filtered? The text says 'the trend mode alone' is plotted, but gives no formula for its slope or monotonicity test; (c) the regime filter ('trend agreement') rejects 589 of 1030 zero crossings for 'disagreeing with the trend mode', yet never defines what 'disagree' means — no threshold, no derivative, no lagged comparison rule is provided. This matches fatal criterion (2): 'rule cannot be written as a precise formula — article gives only general description'.
non_fatal: No out-of-sample testing is performed — but per instructions, absence of OOS test is non-fatal.
No accounting for spread or commissions in reported PnL — per instructions, this is non-fatal.
The 512-bar window is fixed and not optimized per instrument/timeframe — non-fatal, as optimization is our task.
The strategy uses log-transformed prices and maps back to price space — this is valid for spot forex and does not require non-forex data.
No martingale, grid, or averaging is used — position sizing is based on fixed % risk and stop distance, not loss recovery.
This is a trading strategy article (not infrastructure/graphic/optimizer/tutorial) — criterion (5) does not apply.

judge.reject_reason: Фатальный порок: условие входа не может быть записано как полное детерминированное правило. (a) 'пересечение нулевого уровня вверх' не определено формально: нет описания способа обнаружения пересечения (смена знака между барами? интерполяция? порог гистерезиса?), не указано, как обрабатываются плато или множественные пересечения; (b) 'трендовый режим растёт' — не определено: на скольких барах измеряется рост (1, 2, N?), как вычисляется наклон (конечная разность? скользящее среднее производной?), нет формулы; (c) фильтр 'согласование с трендом' отклоняет 589 из 1030 сигналов, но статья не указывает, что именно означает 'несогласование' — ни порога, ни правила сравнения, ни используемого лага. Это делает невозможным воспроизведение условия входа как чёткого, детерминированного правила для проверки на закрытых барах.
judge.summary: Статья представляет библиотеку VMD для MetaTrader 5 с акцентом на каузальность и измерение влияния ретроспективных данных. Описана стратегия, основанная на пересечении осциллирующего режима (ранг 1) нулевого уровня при росте трендового режима, с риск-менеджментом, выводимым из параметров декомпозиции. Однако ключевое условие входа не формализовано до уровня детерминированного правила: отсутствуют точные определения пересечения нуля, критерия «роста тренда» и логики фильтра «согласования», что делает невозможным его однозначную реализацию и проверку.
